abstract.text: We study empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss. The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Other architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range. Simple equations govern the dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size and the dependence of training speed on model size. These relationships allow us to determine the optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget. Larger models are significantly more sampleefficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence.

sections.summary: The paper introduces its central claim that language-model cross-entropy loss obeys power laws in model size, data size, and compute, with weak dependence on architectural shape. It lists the headline findings and gives the main scaling equations for L(N), L(D), L(Cmin), L(N,D), L(N,S), and optimal compute allocation.

sections.summary: Defines notation and the empirical setup: WebText2 data, byte-pair tokenization, decoder-only Transformer models, non-embedding parameter count N, and compute estimate C ≈ 6NBS. It describes training procedures, datasets, and the start of the empirical scaling runs.
sections.title: Notation, model, data, and training setup

source_span.end_text: in all cases the models were trained only on the WebText2 dataset.
source_span.start_text: Empirical Results and Basic Power Laws

sections.summary: Tests architectural shape independence and scaling with non-embedding parameter count N. Performance depends weakly on depth, width, attention heads, and feed-forward ratio when N is fixed, and L(N) follows a power law. It also compares Transformers to LSTMs and begins generalization tests across other data distributions.
sections.title: Shape independence and scaling with model size N

source_span.end_text: The data strongly suggests that sample efficiency improves with model size, and we also illustrate this directly in Figure 19 in the appendix.
source_span.start_text: Performance with Dataset Size and Compute

sections.summary: Introduces dataset-size and compute scaling laws L(D) and L(C), showing power-law trends when dataset or compute is the bottleneck. The data also indicate that sample efficiency improves with model size.

source_span.end_text: The line is our fit to that equation.
source_span.start_text: Charting the Infinite Data Limit and Overfitting

sections.summary: Proposes and fits the joint scaling law L(N,D), which combines model-size and dataset-size bottlenecks and predicts overfitting through the ratio N^{αN/αD}/D. It validates the fit empirically except for the smallest dataset regime.
sections.title: Joint scaling law and overfitting

sections.summary: Explains the critical batch size Bcrit(L), its power-law dependence on loss, and how to adjust training steps and compute to a common Smin and Cmin. This adjustment is needed before fitting joint scaling laws involving training time and compute.
sections.title: Critical batch size and adjusted training steps

source_span.end_text: We also make some brief comparisons to LSTMs and recurrent Transformers [DGV+18].
source_span.start_text: Results for L(N, Smin) and Performance with Model Size and Compute

sections.summary: Fits L(N,Smin) to learning curves in the infinite-data limit and gives parameters αN, αS, Nc, Sc. It shows that fixing compute or steps yields an optimal model size, and derives a lower bound on early-stopping step.
sections.title: Joint scaling with model size and training time

source_span.end_text: Our scaling laws provide a predictive framework for the performance of language modeling.
source_span.start_text: Optimal Allocation of the Compute Budget

sections.summary: Uses L(N,Smin) to derive optimal allocation of compute. The optimal model size grows quickly with compute, N∝Cmin^{0.73}, while batch size and serial steps grow much more slowly, so compute-efficient training should mostly increase model size.
sections.title: Optimal allocation of the compute budget

source_span.end_text: The most obvious interpretation is that our scaling laws break down at or before we reach this point, which is still many orders of magnitude away in both compute and model size.

sections.summary: The compute-efficient and dataset-limited power laws eventually contradict each other because data grows too slowly with compute. The intersection point is conjectured to signal where scaling laws break down and may estimate the entropy-per-token of natural language.
sections.title: Contradiction, data limits, and maximal performance conjecture

source_span.end_text: Big models may be more important than big data.

sections.summary: Places the results in the literature: power-law scaling, model/data scaling, optimal compute allocation, generalization theory, and architecture scaling. The discussion emphasizes that larger models should remain more sample-efficient and that model parallelism may be key.
sections.title: Related work and discussion

source_span.end_text: The optimal parameters for compute efficient training are given by:

sections.summary: Appendix A summarizes all key power-law equations and fitted parameters for L(N), L(D), L(C), L(Cmin), L(N,D), and L(N,S), plus compute-efficient training values.
sections.title: Appendix A: Summary of power laws

source_span.end_text: A 2.2x larger model requires 45% fewer steps at a cost of 20% more training compute.

sections.summary: Appendix B derives the compute-efficient frontier from L(N,S): optimal loss, model size, and steps as functions of compute. It compares efficient training to convergence-focused training and analyzes suboptimal model sizes.
sections.title: Appendix B: Compute-efficient frontier derivation

source_span.end_text: Note that the degree of overfitting (as compared to the infinite data limit) is significantly overestimated by Ltest − Ltrain

sections.summary: Appendix C lists caveats: lack of theory, uncertainty in Bcrit extrapolation, small-data fit limitations, omitted context-dependent compute, hyperparameter tuning gaps, and learning-rate sensitivity.
sections.title: Appendix C: Caveats and limitations

source_span.end_text: Sample efficiency (show here for training far below the critical batch size) improves greatly as well, improving by a factor of almost 100 when comparing the smallest possible model to a very large one.

sections.summary: Appendix D.1–D.4 presents supplemental early-stopping, recurrent Transformer, batch-size scan, and sample-efficiency figures. It measures Bcrit from step-token fits and shows larger models need fewer steps/examples to reach fixed loss.
sections.title: Appendix D.1–D.4: Early stopping, recurrent Transformers, batch size, sample efficiency

source_span.end_text: The 12-layer model overfit the Internet Books dataset and we show the early-stopped performance; we have not seen this surprising result in other experiments.

sections.summary: Appendix D.5–D.8 studies per-token context dependence, learning-rate schedule robustness, power-law versus logarithmic fit quality, and generalization across architectures. It finds predictable per-token power laws, weak schedule dependence, and no depth effect on generalization when parameter count is fixed.
sections.title: Appendix D.5–D.8: Context, learning schedules, fit quality, generalization vs depth

source_span.end_text: Our scaling laws provide a predictive framework for the performance of language modeling.
source_span.start_text: Optimal Allocation of the Compute Budget

sections.summary: Uses L(N,Smin) to derive optimal allocation of compute. The optimal model size grows quickly with compute, N∝Cmin^{0.73}, while batch size and serial steps grow much more slowly, so compute-efficient training should mostly increase model size.
sections.title: Optimal allocation of the compute budget

source_span.end_text: The most obvious interpretation is that our scaling laws break down at or before we reach this point, which is still many orders of magnitude away in both compute and model size.

sections.summary: The compute-efficient and dataset-limited power laws eventually contradict each other because data grows too slowly with compute. The intersection point is conjectured to signal where scaling laws break down and may estimate the entropy-per-token of natural language.
sections.title: Contradiction, data limits, and maximal performance conjecture

source_span.end_text: Big models may be more important than big data.

sections.summary: Places the results in the literature: power-law scaling, model/data scaling, optimal compute allocation, generalization theory, and architecture scaling. The discussion emphasizes that larger models should remain more sample-efficient and that model parallelism may be key.
sections.title: Related work and discussion

source_span.end_text: The optimal parameters for compute efficient training are given by:

sections.summary: Appendix A summarizes all key power-law equations and fitted parameters for L(N), L(D), L(C), L(Cmin), L(N,D), and L(N,S), plus compute-efficient training values.
sections.title: Appendix A: Summary of power laws

source_span.end_text: A 2.2x larger model requires 45% fewer steps at a cost of 20% more training compute.

sections.summary: Appendix B derives the compute-efficient frontier from L(N,S): optimal loss, model size, and steps as functions of compute. It compares efficient training to convergence-focused training and analyzes suboptimal model sizes.
sections.title: Appendix B: Compute-efficient frontier derivation

source_span.end_text: Note that the degree of overfitting (as compared to the infinite data limit) is significantly overestimated by Ltest − Ltrain

sections.summary: Appendix C lists caveats: lack of theory, uncertainty in Bcrit extrapolation, small-data fit limitations, omitted context-dependent compute, hyperparameter tuning gaps, and learning-rate sensitivity.
sections.title: Appendix C: Caveats and limitations

source_span.end_text: Sample efficiency (show here for training far below the critical batch size) improves greatly as well, improving by a factor of almost 100 when comparing the smallest possible model to a very large one.

sections.summary: Appendix D.1–D.4 presents supplemental early-stopping, recurrent Transformer, batch-size scan, and sample-efficiency figures. It measures Bcrit from step-token fits and shows larger models need fewer steps/examples to reach fixed loss.
sections.title: Appendix D.1–D.4: Early stopping, recurrent Transformers, batch size, sample efficiency

source_span.end_text: The 12-layer model overfit the Internet Books dataset and we show the early-stopped performance; we have not seen this surprising result in other experiments.

sections.summary: Appendix D.5–D.8 studies per-token context dependence, learning-rate schedule robustness, power-law versus logarithmic fit quality, and generalization across architectures. It finds predictable per-token power laws, weak schedule dependence, and no depth effect on generalization when parameter count is fixed.
sections.title: Appendix D.5–D.8: Context, learning schedules, fit quality, generalization vs depth
